summary: Analyzes multihoming in IPv6 network mobility (NEMO), where a whole mobile network, such as in a vehicle, may have multiple connections. It proposes a taxonomy of configurations, describes deployment scenarios and issues with NEMO Basic Support, and offers recommendations. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A moving network, like on a bus, might use several internet connections at once. This sorts out the ways it can happen and the problems.

questions: what are the nemo multihoming configurations
subtitle: Sorting out the eight ways a moving network, like a train or a car, can connect to the Internet in several places at once.

tldr.problem: NEMO Basic Support gives a mobile network, such as an in-vehicle network, a tunnel to its home agent, but it says nothing about managing several tunnels when the network is multihomed.
tldr.mechanism: The memo classifies multihomed mobile networks by the number of mobile routers, home agents and mobile network prefixes, then walks through the issues each configuration raises under NEMO Basic Support.
tldr.outcome: It finds issues such as failure detection, ingress filtering, router synchronization and prefix delegation, marks which are NEMO-specific, and recommends which working groups should address them.

today: RFC 4980 is an Informational analysis from October 2007 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It analyzes NEMO Basic Support (RFC 3963) rather than defining a new protocol.

sections.title: Why Multihomed Mobile Networks Matter
sections.content:
NEMO Basic Support (RFC 3963) provides continuous Internet connectivity to nodes in an IPv6 mobile network, for example an in-vehicle network. It sets up bi-directional tunnels between the mobile routers (MRs) and their home agents (HAs), much like Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) does for a single host. Nodes behind the MR do not have to take any action.

Wireless links are less reliable and many nodes sit behind an MR, so losing connectivity hurts more than for one host. Permanent access therefore often needs several interfaces and technologies, such as Wimax, Wifi and 3G. A mobile network is multihomed when an MR has multiple egress interfaces, when there are multiple MRs, when there are multiple HAs, or when multiple global prefixes are available.

NEMO Basic Support does not specify any mechanism to manage multiple tunnels. The memo aims to find the possible configurations, capture the issues, decide which are worth solving and where, and point to potential solutions. It considers only IPv6.
sections.eli5: A bus with Wi-Fi may be plugged into the internet in several ways at once. The rules for the bus's main connection did not explain how to juggle several.

sections.title: A Taxonomy of Eight Configurations
sections.content:
The memo describes each configuration by a 3-tuple (x,y,z). The value x is the number of mobile routers, y is the number of home agents, and z is the number of mobile network prefixes (MNPs). Each is either 1 or n (more than one), giving 8 combinations, from (1,1,1) to (n,n,n).

In every case the MR itself may be multihomed, if it has multiple interfaces or multiple prefixes are available, and then it has multiple (HoA,CoA) pairs with one bi-directional tunnel per pair. The nodes behind the MR (MNNs) are multihomed only when several MNPs are available, since they then configure an address from each one.

The memo gives examples. A car whose personal traffic uses a prefix from home and whose maintenance traffic uses one from the manufacturer is typically (1,1,n) or (1,n,n). A train with one MR per car sharing one HA is an (n,1,*) configuration, and a transatlantic flight with an HA on each continent is (1,n,1) if there is only one MR. Appendix A outlines two alternative classifications, ownership-oriented and problem-oriented.
sections.eli5: Count three things: how many gateways the vehicle has, how many home helpers back them up, and how many address ranges the passengers get. Each count is either one or many.

sections.title: Goals and What Multihoming Needs
sections.content:
The memo takes six generic multihoming goals from another document: permanent and ubiquitous access, reliability, load sharing, load balancing and flow distribution, preference settings, and aggregate bandwidth.

Meeting them has prerequisites. At least one bi-directional tunnel must be available at all times. Reliability needs traffic to be diverted to another tunnel when one breaks, which does not by itself need several simultaneous tunnels. Load sharing, load balancing, preference settings and aggregate bandwidth need several tunnels maintained at once. Where preferences are used, users, applications and administrators should be told about the available tunnels and be able to set preferences.
sections.eli5: To keep the internet always on, you need at least one working road. To use several roads for speed, you must keep them all open at once.

sections.title: Fault Tolerance and Path Handling
sections.content:
Fault tolerance breaks into four tasks: failure detection, path exploration, path selection and re-homing. How hard each is depends on the configuration. With a single HA, only the MRs and that HA are involved. With multiple HAs in different networks, an end-to-end mechanism may be needed, and the memo says Shim6 protocols may help in the (n,n,n) case.

Detecting a tunnel failure is hard on the HA side, because no standardized tunnel liveness protocol exists. One suggestion is to have MRs send binding updates more often with shorter Lifetime values, or have HAs return smaller Lifetimes, so binding updates act as tunnel heartbeats. The cost is more traffic and processing, because binding updates must be protected by security associations.

Path selection can be done by the HA, the MR, the nodes behind the MR, the user or application, or a combination. Tunnels can run primary-secondary, with one default and others as backup, or peer-to-peer with equal priority. For most of these issues the memo concludes that a Mobile IPv6 solution should also apply to NEMO.
sections.eli5: If one road breaks, you need to notice it, look for another road, choose one and move your trip onto it. Each step is harder when there are many roads and many helpers.

sections.title: Other Multihoming Issues
sections.content:
The memo studies more issues beyond fault tolerance.

  • Ingress filtering. A packet whose source address comes from one MNP may be dropped if it is tunneled to an HA that does not handle that prefix. This is hardest in the (n,n,n) case. Suggested approaches are source address dependent routing, nested tunnels, or deprecating prefixes tied to unavailable exit routers.
  • HA and MR synchronization. Several HAs or MRs may need to coordinate, for example to advertise the same prefix. No standardized router-to-router synchronization protocol is known.
  • Prefix delegation. When one MNP is advertised along several paths, there is no synchronization mechanism, so MRs may announce incompatible prefixes.
  • Source address selection and preference settings. Nodes with several addresses lack the information to choose well, and in the (1,n,1) case they cannot influence path selection at all.
  • Loop prevention and prefix ownership. A multihomed network nested in another may no longer form a tree, risking loops. When a (n,*,1) network splits, MRs on separate links may both try to register the only MNP.
sections.eli5: Some other problems: a guard may reject a letter with the wrong return address, helpers must agree on which address range to hand out, and two groups might both claim the same one.

sections.title: Recommendations and Conclusion
sections.content:
A matrix in the memo marks each issue per configuration as NEMO specific, MIPv6 specific, generic IPv6 or Shim6 related. NEMO-specific concerns include failure detection, path exploration, path selection, re-homing, ingress filtering, HA synchronization, prefix delegation, loop prevention and prefix ownership.

The authors recommend that solutions for failure detection, path exploration, path selection and re-homing be solicited from other working groups such as Monami6 or Shim6. Ingress filtering in the (n,n,n) case can be solved by the NEMO working group, and HA synchronization belongs in a mobility-specific group. Multiple bindings are being handled by Monami6, prefix delegation proposals should be reviewed, loop prevention needs research, and vendors and operators should weigh in on prefix ownership.

The Security Considerations note that security of these configurations must be considered by forthcoming solutions if it differs from NEMO Basic Support. As an example, an attacker could try to use the multihomed device to reach another network that would not normally be reachable.
sections.eli5: The authors sorted the problems into piles and said which team of experts should fix each pile.
